in.other_title: Majority voting performs on par with multi-agent debate in most cases
in.rationale: Du et al.'s results table has the rows Single Agent, Single Agent (Reflection), Multi-Agent (Majority) and Multi-Agent (Debate) and the columns Arithmetic (%), Grade School Math (%) and Chess (∆PS), and the cited lines then list eight scores from 67.0 ± 4.7 to 85.0 ± 3.5, so Du et al. compare multi-agent debate with multi-agent majority voting. Choi, Zhu and Li report that majority voting performs on par with MAD in most cases and say these findings suggest that MAD's effectiveness is largely driven by model ensembling rather than the iterative debate process itself.

in.other_title: Authors argue prior reported MAD gains over majority voting may partly reflect answer parsing
in.rationale: Choi et al. note that prior works [2, 3, 10] reported consistent gains from MAD over majority voting, and argue that these results may be partially driven by error-prone rule-based answer extraction that can mark correct responses as incorrect. Their reference list gives [2] as Yilun Du et al., 'Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate', the to-record's paper. In that paper Du et al. compare their approach with three alternative approaches, the last being generating responses with multiple agents and performing majority voting, and report in Table 1 that multiagent debate, which may be seen as a combination of reflection and multiagent generation, gives a substantial boost in reasoning across arithmetic, grade school math and chess. Choi et al.'s argument therefore bears on the gains [2] reports, as a possible flaw in how they were measured, though the argument is hedged ('may be partially driven'), the cited passage reports no rerun of Du et al.'s experiments, and it does not show which answer extraction Du et al. used.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Du et al.'s ([2] in Choi et al.) Table 1 claim that multiagent debate gives a substantial boost in reasoning on arithmetic, grade school math and chess, where the baselines include majority voting over multiple agents; Choi et al. argue that prior reported MAD gains over majority voting, including those of [2], may be partially driven by error-prone final-answer extraction

text: In Table 1 the authors report results on arithmetic, grade school math and chess reasoning tasks, mainly using three ChatGPT-based agents with two rounds of debate. In each task, using multiple agents to generate solutions improves performance over a single agent, reflection generally gives a modest boost, and multiagent debate, which may be seen as a combination of reflection and multiagent generation, gives a substantial boost in reasoning across each of the tasks.
title: Multiagent debate gives a substantial reasoning boost on arithmetic, grade school math and chess
